newsitem.title: UK: Privatisations key to '95 "lumpy" Latam FDI - UNCTAD.
newsitem.headline: Privatisations key to '95 "lumpy" Latam FDI - UNCTAD.

text.p: Privatisations in Latin America were the main attraction for foreign direct investment (FDI) in 1995 but inflows to the region were "lumpy", the latest World Investment Report from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said.
Inflows to Latin America and the Caribbean rose by five percent in 1995 to $427 billion over 1994, and represented a quarter of all FDI to developing countries.
Investment was concentrated in Mexico, Brazil, Chile, Argentina and Peru, the report said.

"FDI to individual countries in the region is greatly influenced by the timing of large-scale transactions such as a major privatisation...therefore there are large year-to-year fluctuations, which makes them lumpy," UNCTAD said.
Sectors most affected tended to be infrastructure, mining and petrochemical industries and UNCTAD sees little change to the trend in coming years.

But it cautioned that potential investors should look at several years' data to get a good picture of the country or industry. "Averaging values of FDI flows over several years can smooth some of the lumpiness." The largest recipients of FDI in 1995 were Mexico ($7.0 billion/$8.0 billion in 1994), Brazil ($4.9 billion/$3.1 billion), Argentina ($3.9 billion/$1.2 billion), Chile ($3.0 billion/$2.5 billion), Bermuda ($2.9 billion/$2.9 billion) and Colombia ($1.2 billion/$1.7 billion).
The largest investors were Brazil ($1.4 billion), Chile, Bahamas and Mexico (all $0.6 billion), Venezuela ($0.5 billion) and Colombia ($0.1 billion).

A number of transnational corporations in Latin America rank in the top 50 from developing coutnries. The list is toppped by Mexico's Cemex, with a total $7.8 billion in assets, $2.8 billion classified as foreign holdings.
Grupo Televisa SA de CV. a Mexican media group, is second, followed by Brazil's Souza Cruz SA and Petrobras.

The intra-regional investment which is so marked in Asia is not present to the same degree in Latin America, but the Mercosur economic group was helping develop it, an UNCTAD official said at a briefing on the report in London.

He said it was important for developing countries to build up their own transnational corporations because according to UNCTAD estimates, they usually manage to translate $1 foreign stock into $3 of sales.
